PMGT1852 Week 08

PMGT1852 Week 8 - Networks and Stakeholder Engagement

From relationships to engagement decisions

Social network analysis (SNA) examines actors and the relations connecting them. For stakeholder engagement, it adds a structural perspective: a person's influence may depend on their position in information and problem-solving relationships, not just their formal role or others' perceptions of their power.

A stakeholder is a person or group that can affect or be affected by the work. An actor is a person or organisation represented as a network node, and a tie is a measured relationship between actors. A sociogram visualises actors as nodes and ties as lines or arrows.

Three levels of network thinking

Level

Theoretical anchor

Constructs

Relevance to stakeholder engagement

Network

Bavelas' communication-network experiments at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT)

Density and centralisation

Assess overall connectedness and the extent to which relationships are concentrated around a central actor

Actor

Freeman's centrality concepts and Burt's structural-hole theory

Degree, betweenness, closeness and constraint

Identify direct information access, brokerage potential, independence of access and limits on reach

Tie

Granovetter's strength-of-weak-ties theory

Tie strength

Examine the nature and strength of a relationship and its role in information access or coordinated work

Network-level concepts

• Density is the proportion of possible ties that actually exist. High density means many actors are connected to one another; low density means relatively few such connections.

• Centralisation is the extent to which a network's connections or other centrality values are concentrated around a small number of actors. It describes the network, not the centrality of a single person.

A large sociogram can contain dense local clusters and a more sparsely connected centre. Overall density alone can therefore conceal meaningful local patterns.

Actor-level concepts

Construct

Meaning

Engagement interpretation

Degree centrality

Number of direct ties

Potential for high direct information flow

Betweenness centrality

Extent to which an actor lies on shortest paths between others

Brokerage or gatekeeping potential

Closeness centrality

Short-path accessibility to other actors

Potential independence from intermediaries when reaching others

Constraint

Extent to which an actor's relationships lead back into the same interconnected circle

Lack of reach into independent, non-redundant contacts

High degree does not guarantee that information actually flows, and high betweenness does not prove deliberate control. These measures indicate structural opportunities or dependencies.

A structural hole is a gap between actors or groups that are not directly connected. A broker bridges that gap. Burt's framework highlights access to non-redundant information: connections into the same tightly interconnected group may offer less novelty than connections to otherwise separate groups. High constraint limits such independent access.

Tie-level concepts

Weak ties can act as bridges carrying new information into a tightly connected group. Strong ties can support trust, shared understanding and the coordination needed to solve complex problems.

The distinction is functional rather than a ranking of good and bad relationships. Information discovery and difficult implementation may require different combinations of weak and strong ties. Not every weak tie necessarily bridges groups, and a strong tie can also carry new information.

Rowley's structural classification of stakeholder influence

Rowley's 1997 framework combines stakeholder centrality with the density of the surrounding stakeholder network.

Stakeholder-network density

Low stakeholder centrality

High stakeholder centrality

High

Subordinate

Compromiser

Low

Solitarian

Commander

• Commander: high centrality in a low-density setting. Other actors have relatively few connections to one another, so the focal actor has greater scope to coordinate or broker exchanges between them. This indicates potential leverage, not proof of being the only possible channel.

• Compromiser: high centrality in a high-density setting. The focal actor is well connected, but others can also coordinate independently, encouraging negotiation rather than unilateral control.

• Subordinate: low centrality in a high-density setting. Other actors can coordinate without the focal actor, limiting its structural influence.

• Solitarian: low centrality in a low-density setting. The focal actor has few connections and limited integration into collective activity.

This differs from an attribute-based assessment. A salience model assesses power, legitimacy and urgency; a power-interest grid compares power with interest. Rowley's classification asks about position within a pattern of relationships. The approaches measure different aspects of stakeholder importance.

ACME Telco case

Organisation and network boundary

ACME Telco is an internet service provider in Tasmania, established in 2008. The case describes 31 employees serving more than 100 small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs). There were 27 employee respondents, a reported response rate of 87%.

The relationship studied was interaction for problem-solving in project work over the preceding three months. A name-generator question asks respondents to identify relevant contacts; here it asked who they interacted with for problem-solving matters during that period.

This is an internal whole-network, or sociocentric, design because the organisational boundary is defined. Having 27 respondents does not necessarily restrict the set of rated or nominated actors to 27: respondents may identify other members of the 31-person boundary. The available data do not establish every detail of how non-response was handled.

Measurements

Participants rated their own project interest and influence, as well as the interest and influence of nominated colleagues. The power-interest grid uses other-rated power and other-rated interest, meaning colleagues' perceptions rather than only self-ratings.

The structural model uses:

• Problem-solving betweenness centrality: an actor's position on shortest paths in the measured problem-solving network.

• Ego density: connectedness among the focal actor's contacts. It is a local measure and is not automatically identical to the density of the whole organisational network.

Analysis process

Communicate with the company and define the enquiry.

Survey participants and collect relational and rating data.

Analyse the data using network and spreadsheet tools.

Interpret the measures and construct classification grids.

Compare the classifications and consider engagement implications.

UCINET is software for social network analysis, NetDraw visualises networks, and Excel supports tabulation and grid construction. Software output still requires interpretation of the network boundary, relation and missing data.

Visualising stakeholder attributes and relations

An illustrative stakeholder sociogram places Team Leader 1 at a prominent hub, connected to actors including team members John, May and Kay; a sponsor; Banker A; a project manager; Councilor A; a community representative; Competitor A; manufacturers A and B; suppliers A-D; and customers A-D.

Node shape distinguishes organisational affiliation, node colour distinguishes power-interest categories, and line thickness represents tie strength. Example affiliation labels include Accupoint, ACME, Cancer Council, CBA, DBA, Hyundai, IMB, Noogle, Potus, Sydney Council and Telstar. These are case labels, not an established list of the internal survey's 31 employees. Their presence should not be used to infer a larger internal survey sample or an unreported network boundary.

The visualisation demonstrates how actor attributes and relational data can be displayed together. A central-looking position on a drawing is not by itself a computed centrality result.

Only five of the twelve Manage Closely actors are listed as Commanders. Conversely, three Monitor actors, 12, 16 and 26, have Commander positions in the structural model. People perceived as low power and low interest can therefore occupy important problem-solving paths.

Implications for engagement

Attribute-based and structural assessments should be used together rather than treated as competing versions of the same measure.

Assess formal roles, perceived power, interest and legitimate claims.

Examine actual problem-solving, advice or communication relationships.

Investigate disagreements between the two assessments.

Check whether highly connected actors are bottlenecks, under-recognised brokers or useful connectors.

Tailor engagement to the relationship and the work required, not just the actor's label.

Reassess after interventions or changes in the project.

A low-power label should not be grounds for ignoring evidence of informal influence. Equally, centrality does not replace ethical consideration of affected people with limited network access. A sound engagement plan considers both structural leverage and stakeholder needs.
